title: The Build vs Buy Framework for Engineering Leaders
author: Karol Wójciszko
summary: Wójciszko takes apart the core-versus-context heuristic that engineering leaders recite when deciding whether to build or buy, and replaces it with a decision process he actually uses. His objection to the standard rule is not that it is wrong but that it sounds cleaner in a conference talk than in a real org, where the obviously contextual thing sometimes turns out to matter more than the core. Instead of scoring a spreadsheet he pictures two futures, one where the team built and one where it bought, and asks which he would rather be living in six months out. Six questions carry the decision: how long he is willing to wait, what the arithmetic on engineer-hours against license fees says, who specifically owns the thing after it ships, whether the tool will still fit once the product has moved, what the team is not shipping instead, and whether the idea can be validated cheaply first. The fifth question is the one he treats as the deciding vote, on the grounds that engineering time spent building is pulled from the same finite pool as everything else on the roadmap. He offers his own greenlit in-house reporting module as the cautionary case, where the real cost was the customer-facing feature that sat untouched in the backlog. The closing case studies sit behind a paywall.
points: Timeline can end the debate before cost enters it, because a better long-term solution that lands a quarter late helps nobody.
Unassigned ownership is a strike against building: if the leader cannot name who owns the thing in a year, it will quietly rot.
Vendor tools should be judged against the product's trajectory rather than today's requirements, or the team pays for the migration twice.
The real comparison is not build against buy but build against everything else the team could have shipped in the same quarter.
Cheap AI-generated proof-of-concepts now run by default before a real build is greenlit, purely to test whether the idea works.
quotes: On paper it looks like a simple cost comparison. In practice, it’s one of the decisions I see leaders get wrong most often - because the “obvious” rule everyone quotes has way more exceptions than people admit.
Core means the thing you actually make money from. The unique algorithm, the proprietary workflow, whatever your product literally is.
I weigh this one heavily, more than most people expect, because a “better” long-term solution that arrives too late doesn’t actually help anyone.
But here’s what I actually pay attention to: if we build, does that maintenance land on someone specific, or does it land on “whoever has time,” which in practice means nobody?
So the real comparison isn’t “build this feature” versus “buy this feature.” It’s “build this feature” versus “everything else my team could have shipped in that same quarter.
Every hour spent building something we could have bought is an hour not spent on the thing our customers actually asked for.

None of these six questions alone will make the decision for you. But run through all of them honestly, weighting the ones that actually matter for your situation, and the right call usually becomes obvious.
